document_check.note: Devlin KN, Brennan L, Saad L, et al. Diagnosing Mild Cognitive Impairment Among Racially Diverse Older Adults: Comparison of Consensus, Actuarial, and Statistical Methods. J Alzheimers Dis 2022;85(2):627-644 (PMC author manuscript). N = 354; MCI rates 44% (consensus), 53% (actuarial), 41% (LCA); race comparisons as cited.

cited_result: Baseline MCI classification of the same 354 participants by three definitions: consensus 44%, actuarial (Jak/Bondi) 53%, latent class analysis 41%; with the Black versus White comparison by definition (consensus 27% v 51%, LCA 30% v 46%, actuarial 54% v 52%; N = 343). Principal result appraised: the between-definition divergence in MCI rates, with the race-by-definition comparison assessed alongside because it comes from the same baseline data.
tool_reason: The cited result compares classification rates across definitions and between racial groups at a single (baseline) time point in a clinic research cohort; it is neither a prediction model nor a population prevalence estimate.

domains.domain: Item 1: Criteria for inclusion in the sample clearly defined
domains.rationale: Four explicit inclusion criteria are stated. Inclusion required a consensus NC or MCI diagnosis, so the actuarial and LCA definitions were applied within a consensus-defined sample.

signalling.question: Were the criteria for inclusion in the sample clearly defined?
signalling.quote: Inclusion criteria for the present study were 1) complete data for all 14 cognitive measures of interest (see below) at one or more visits, the earliest of which was classified as the baseline visit; 2) age 55 or older at baseline; 3) English as primary language; and 4) clinical consensus diagnosis of normal cognition (NC) or MCI at baseline.

domains.domain: Item 2: Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.rationale: Setting (Penn ADC Clinical Core), recruitment routes, age range, race and education are reported.

signalling.question: Were the study subjects and the setting described in detail?
signalling.quote: The present sample was comprised of 354 older adults who completed cognitive testing as part of the Alzheimer’s Disease Center Clinical Core at the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania [47]. Participants were enrolled through a combination of clinician referral, self-referral, and community recruitment.

signalling.question: Were the study subjects and the setting described in detail? (demographics)
signalling.quote: Participants ranged in age from 55–93. Most participants identified as White (68%), and Black participants were well represented (29%), but other racial and ethnic groups were not.

domains.domain: Item 3: Exposure measured validly and reliably
domains.rationale: The exposures (definition applied; self-identified race) are explicitly operationalised: a fixed actuarial rule, a consensus of at least two clinicians, and a specified LCA procedure applied to the same test data.

signalling.question: Was the exposure (diagnostic definition applied) measured in a valid and reliable way?
signalling.quote: Participants were classified as having MCI if they had an impaired score, defined as > 1 SD below the normative mean, on two or more measures within a cognitive domain.

signalling.question: Was the exposure (consensus method) measured in a valid and reliable way?
signalling.quote: Clinical diagnosis was determined by the consensus of at least two clinicians using all available clinical information, including demographics, comprehensive neuropsychological data, functional status, medical and psychiatric history, and neuroimaging.

domains.domain: Item 4: Objective, standard criteria for the condition
domains.rationale: Consensus diagnosis follows published MCI criteria and the actuarial method follows published Jak/Bondi criteria. The consensus 'impaired score' threshold is not a fixed cut-off, and the MCI or normal labels for LCA classes are interpretive, but both are described.

signalling.question: Were objective, standard criteria used for measurement of the condition?
signalling.quote: MCI was diagnosed in the presence of 1) subjective report of cognitive decline, 2) an impaired score, accounting for demographics and background, on at least one cognitive test, and 3) preservation of everyday functioning [58, 59].

signalling.question: Were objective, standard criteria used for measurement of the condition? (actuarial)
signalling.quote: Actuarial diagnoses were made using the “comprehensive neuropsychological criteria” approach [9, 10].

domains.rationale: Education, literacy and differential selection and survival by race are identified.

signalling.question: Were confounding factors identified?
signalling.quote: Black participants (M = 14.3, SD = 3.7) had significantly fewer years of education than White participants (M = 16.5, SD = 2.6), with a medium effect size (p < 0.001, η2p = 0.132). The difference in literacy/academic achievement was more pronounced.

signalling.question: Were confounding factors identified? (selection)
signalling.quote: Selection and survival biases likely differentially influenced enrollment and retention of Black and White participants in the present study, and results should be interpreted with this caveat.

domains.domain: Item 6: Strategies to deal with confounding stated
domains.rationale: The comparison between definitions is within the same participants, so person-level confounding does not apply. Demographic influences on test scores were handled by normative adjustment, with a race-adjusted sensitivity analysis. The Black versus White comparison, however, is an unadjusted chi-squared test. Literacy (education quality) and recruitment route were identified as differing by race but were not addressed.

signalling.question: Were strategies to deal with confounding factors stated?
signalling.quote: For all primary analyses, raw scores were converted to z-scores adjusted for age, education, and gender [57]. A second set of analyses was conducted with z-scores adjusted for age, education, gender, and race [57].

signalling.question: Were strategies to deal with confounding factors stated? (race comparison analysis)
signalling.quote: Differences in race/ethnicity by diagnostic category were examined using Pearson’s chi-squared test.

signalling.question: Were strategies to deal with confounding factors stated? (literacy)
signalling.quote: Whether the use of education quality-based normative adjustments improves diagnostic concordance and prognostic validity in this sample is a topic of future study.

domains.domain: Item 7: Outcomes measured validly and reliably
domains.rationale: Each method was applied to the same full test data by a specified procedure. The actuarial rule is fully reproducible. LCA used standard fit indices and reports acceptable entropy, although the choice of five classes involved judgement. No inter-rater reliability is reported for consensus.

signalling.question: Were the outcomes (MCI classifications) measured in a valid and reliable way?
signalling.quote: A one-class model was examined, and the number of classes was then increased one class at a time until there was no additional improvement in model fit.

signalling.question: Was LCA classification reliable?
signalling.quote: Classification accuracy (entropy) was acceptable for the five-class solution. Finally, the heterogeneity of cognition among non-demented elders is well-supported and clinically meaningful [69–73]. Thus, we interpreted the five-class solution based on a preponderance of evidence from fit statistics, theory, and empirical support.

domains.rationale: Chi-squared tests and kappa for agreement and chi-squared tests for the race comparison, with test statistics reported, suit the descriptive cross-sectional question.

signalling.question: Was appropriate statistical analysis used?
signalling.quote: Agreement of MCI diagnostic methods was examined using chi-squared tests and kappa statistics.

signalling.question: Was appropriate statistical analysis used? (race)
signalling.quote: Black participants were less likely than White participants to be diagnosed with MCI by consensus [27% versus 51%; χ2 (1, N = 343) = 16.18, p < 0.001] and by LCA [30% versus 46%, χ2 (1, N = 343) = 6.89, p = 0.009].

applicability.rationale: The sample is a memory-centre research cohort (clinician referral, self-referral and community volunteers) that is highly educated. It was preselected to consensus NC or MCI, so the absolute rates of 44%, 53% and 41% are sample-specific, not population prevalences.

overall: Some concerns (review rule for the JBI analytical cross-sectional checklist: 7 items Yes, item 6 Unclear)
overall_rationale: The divergence between definitions is measured within the same participants using explicit, published procedures, and the analysis is appropriate. For the race comparison, the authors identify confounding by literacy and by differential selection into the clinic sample but do not address it in the analysis, so the confounding strategy is Unclear.
